analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in full, ending its coverage, protections, and taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the ACA in full was introduced with 2 cosponsors, referred to eight House committees, and has seen no action since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 reconciliation law, effective October 1, 2025, and restores the law as it existed before 2010. That would end the ACA's premium subsidies, its Medicaid expansion, its protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and its requirement that insurers cover essential benefits. It would also erase the taxes the ACA placed on high-income households, large employer plans, medical devices, and tanning services. The bill also undoes the education provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, which included changes to federal student loans.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most directly: repeal restores pre-2010 tax law, eliminating the 3.8% surtax on investment income and the additional Medicare payroll tax that applied above roughly $200,000 of wages, both created by the ACA. Medical device manufacturers and tanning businesses would no longer owe the ACA's excise taxes. Insurers would shed the individual mandate's rules and the medical loss ratio requirement, though they would also lose millions of subsidized customers. Young, healthy people who choose to go uninsured would no longer face a penalty-style incentive to buy coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Repeal restores pre-2010 law, ending the ACA's 3.8% net investment income surtax and the additional Medicare payroll tax on high earners, which fell on households with wages above $200,000 and on investment income.
Repeal removes the ACA's excise taxes, including the medical device excise tax and the tanning services tax, once the pre-2010 code is restored.
Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 undoes that act's changes to federal student aid law, restoring prior loan rules.
Repeal eliminates the individual mandate and ACA insurance market rules, so people who prefer to buy cheaper, skimpier plans or go uninsured face no federal incentive or requirement otherwise.

analysis.who_pays: Millions of people who rely on the ACA lose its benefits: premium tax credits that make marketplace plans affordable, the Medicaid expansion that covered low-income adults, guaranteed coverage regardless of pre-existing conditions, essential health benefits like maternity and prescription drug coverage, the requirement that children stay on a parent's plan until 26, and out-of-pocket caps. Seniors would again pay full drug costs in the Medicare 'donut hole' gap, which the ACA had been closing. Insurers and hospitals would also lose revenue as millions of paying or publicly covered patients become uninsured.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and ACA enrollees

drawbacks.text: The Congressional Budget Office previously estimated ACA repeal would leave millions more uninsured; ending the premium tax credits, Medicaid expansion, and market rules means marketplace plans become unaffordable or unavailable for people with pre-existing conditions or low incomes, and insurers could once again deny or price them out of coverage.

Restoring pre-2010 law also unwinds consumer protections widely used, including the rule allowing young adults to stay on a parent's insurance until age 26 and the ban on annual and lifetime coverage limits.

Because the bill restores 'the provisions of law amended or repealed' by the ACA, it would rewrite large swaths of the Medicare, Medicaid, and tax codes retroactively to 2010 law in one stroke, a change even critics of the ACA generally pursued through narrower replacement legislation rather than full repeal.
The bill offers no replacement plan; it repeals only, so everyone who loses coverage bears the cost immediately with nothing substituted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax relief for high-income households and a few taxed industries is concentrated and easy to quantify, while the costs fall broadly: millions of people lose subsidies, expanded Medicaid, and protections that determine whether they can buy insurance at all. An honest weighing finds the losses far exceed the gains, and the bill's design makes them worse — it repeals without any replacement or transition, so the protections most popular with the public disappear along with the taxes most unpopular with high earners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to eight committees on the day the new Congress convened, and it has sat there with no hearings, no markup, and no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, the opening day of the 119th Congress, with two Republican cosponsors.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations Committees.
No further action has been taken; the bill has received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Affordable Care Act, its subsidies, and its protections remain in effect. High-income households continue paying the ACA's taxes — and everyone covered by the law keeps coverage the bill would have taken away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA beneficiaries; the repeal went nowhere

for.name: Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full ACA repeal bill on the first day of the 119th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Republican, and no Democrat supported the bill.

industries.note: Repeal removes the ACA's rules (guaranteed issue, essential benefits, medical loss ratio) but also strips away the premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion that made insurers tens of millions of paying customers. The bill offers no replacement channel, so the industry's guaranteed role in covering people ends rather than being entrenched.

Repeal eliminates the 3.8% net investment income surtax and the additional Medicare payroll tax on wages above roughly $200,000, both dedicated in part to funding the ACA's coverage expansions. The tax cut flows to the top while the coverage loss falls on lower- and middle-income enrollees.
Restoring pre-2010 law ends the ACA's 2.3% excise tax on medical device sales. The tax had been repeatedly suspended, but this bill would erase it permanently.
Hospitals gained as uninsured rates fell under the ACA; repeal reverses that, sending more unpaid emergency and charity care their way and straining rural and safety-net facilities.

analysis.trajectory: With two cosponsors, no hearing or markup in any of its eight committees, and no vote in nearly a year, the bill has the profile of a message bill that will die in committee when the Congress ends in January 2027. Full repeal also failed when Republicans held both chambers in 2017 with a larger House margin, and the House majority has not scheduled it.
